prompt: A persistent tree inserts a new leaf by path copying. Which existing nodes need copies?

options.text: No existing nodes: only the new leaf needs allocating.
options.explanation: Its ancestors need changed child links, which cannot be written into shared old nodes.

options.text: The ancestors whose child links change, while untouched subtrees can remain shared.
options.explanation: Correct. A new root reaches the copied path and the shared subtrees away from the changed path.

options.text: Every node in every saved version.
options.explanation: Unchanged immutable subtrees can be shared.

options.text: Only nodes smaller than the inserted key, regardless of the search path.
options.explanation: Copying follows changed links, not all keys satisfying a comparison.

workedExample: Insert the new leaf, then construct copies of the ancestors that must point towards it. Keep their untouched child subtrees shared. Both roots remain usable because old nodes were not changed. Extra work is proportional to the changed path; logarithmic cost needs a balanced tree and any rebalancing must also preserve old versions.

prompt: For a balanced n-node tree with one point update per version and n an upper bound on version sizes, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Readers need no mutation locks for immutable nodes that are safely published and kept alive
options.explanation: Immutability removes concurrent mutations, but root publication and safe memory reclamation still require a correct synchronisation protocol.

options.text: Mutating one node in place can silently corrupt several versions at once
options.explanation: Correct. Shared nodes belong to every version that references them, so an in-place write changes all of them.

options.text: Each new version of a balanced tree costs O(log n) extra memory with path copying
options.explanation: Correct. Only the nodes on one root-to-leaf path are new; the rest is shared.

options.text: Keeping v versions necessarily requires Θ(n·v) memory
options.explanation: That is the cost of full copies. Path copying needs memory growing only with n plus v times the logarithm of n (worked through below).

options.text: PostgreSQL's MVCC is an example of path copying
options.explanation: PostgreSQL keeps old row versions in the table heap and removes them with VACUUM. That is versioning at row level, not copying tree paths. LMDB's copy-on-write B-tree is closer.

workedExample: Immutable nodes may be shared by many roots, so changing one in place corrupts those versions. Path copying allocates only the affected logarithmic path in a balanced n-node tree; keeping v versions needs the initial tree plus those added paths, rather than v full copies. Readers still need safely published roots and protected node lifetimes. PostgreSQL’s retained row versions are a different mechanism from tree-path copying.
